[The Shape of a Sound](../instruments-as-operators/index.qmd) · [2 · From the instrument to your ear →](../from-instrument-to-ear/index.qmd) · [Glossary](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd)

::: {.pageinfo}
Start here: this post builds on nothing. Uses sines and fractions; one proof, in a fold, uses integrals and divisibility. About 20 minutes with every demo. Written in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.
:::

A musical sound is a sum of fading pure tones, and its pitch, loudness, timbre and duration are read off their frequencies, sizes and fading times.

**Sound** is the air pressure $p(t)$ at your ear at time $t$, measured from the average air pressure. An instrument plucked or struck and then left to ring sounds, to a good approximation,
$$
p(t) = \sum_n c_n e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n).
$$
Term $n$ is a [partial](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#partial): a pure tone, like a tuning fork's, with frequency $f_n$ in [hertz](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hertz) (cycles per second), numbered from the lowest, starting size $c_n$ and phase $\varphi_n$, the point in its cycle where it starts. It shrinks by a factor of $e \approx 2.7$ every $\tau_n$ seconds, its *fading time*. For a plucked or struck note, each partial comes from one of the instrument's [modes](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#mode), a shape the object swings in at one frequency. A bowed or blown note is the same sum without the fading, for as long as the player keeps going ([route 4 below](#four-routes)).

## Timbre, in the smallest example {#timbre}

Sounds with the same pitch, the same power (so roughly the same loudness) and the same length can still sound different: that difference is timbre.[^timbredef]

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-s="tPure">▶ Pure tone</button><button class="primary" data-s="tBright">▶ All partials, sizes 1/n</button><button class="primary" data-s="tHollow">▶ Odd partials only</button><button class="primary" data-s="tPluck">▶ All partials, plucked</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Four sounds at 220 Hz. The first three are steady, with the same power, and differ only in the sizes: one partial; eight partials at 1, 2, …, 8 times 220 Hz with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/8, which sounds brighter, since strong high partials sound bright; and only the odd ones of those, which sounds hollow, like a clarinet. The fourth has the second's partials but starts suddenly and fades, the higher ones faster, like a pluck: the start, or attack, is a strong cue for naming an instrument (the evidence is in the fold below).</p>
</div>
</div>
```

Besides the sizes $c_n$, timbre depends on how far the $f_n$ sit from whole-number multiples and on noise and transients that are not modes and so lie outside the formula, such as bow noise, breath and a hammer's thump. It also depends on a pattern in the $c_n$ from note to note: fixed resonances, such as a violin's body or a clarinet's tone-hole cutoff, favor the same bands of frequency whatever note is played, so the $c_n$ follow frequency rather than $n$ ([formants](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#formant)).[^formants] The phases $\varphi_n$ matter much less: the ear splits a steady sound into its partials (Ohm's acoustic law),[^ohm] and changing their phases changes the waveform but the timbre far less than changing their sizes does.[^phase]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The evidence for the start, and the formants</summary>

Removing the onsets of recorded instrument tones cut listeners' accuracy at naming the instruments by about 15 percentage points (E. Saldanha and J. F. Corso, ["Timbre cues and the identification of musical instruments"](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1919317), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 36 (1964), 2021–2026, as summarized in K. Siedenburg, [Specifying the perceptual relevance of onset transients for musical instrument identification](https://www.uni-oldenburg.de/f/6/dept/mediphysik/ag/musik-wahrnehmung/siedenburg2019transients.pdf), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 145 (2019), 1078–1087). Listeners also hear a finger hitting a piano key and the key hitting bottom (W. Goebl, R. Bresin and I. Fujinaga, [Perception of touch quality in piano tones](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.4896461), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 136 (2014), 2839–2850). A violin's body favors certain bands of frequency whatever the note, as a voice's formants do (M. Schleske, [Introduction to violin acoustics: sound](https://schleske.de/en/research/introduction-violin-acoustics/introduction/sound.html)). Above a cutoff frequency, roughly 1 to 1.5 kHz on a clarinet, sound waves travel on past the open tone holes instead of being turned back by them, and that cutoff depends little on the fingering (E. Moers and J. Kergomard, "On the cutoff frequency of clarinet-like instruments. Geometrical versus acoustical regularity", *Acta Acustica united with Acustica* 97 (2011), 984–996, [arXiv:1101.4742](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.4742); J. Wolfe and colleagues, [Clarinet acoustics: F3](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/music/clarinet/F3.html), UNSW).

</details>
:::

## The four aspects, in a mixer {#four-aspects}

Each of the four things we hear, a perception measured by asking listeners,[^aspects] has its own control in the mixer below.

- **Pitch**, how high or low the sound is: the common base of the $f_n$, the largest frequency of which they are all (nearly) whole-number multiples, set by the base frequency $f$. It is often $f_1$, but not when no partial sits at it ([below](#missing-fundamental)).
- **Loudness**, how strong the sound seems: the overall size of the $c_n$, set by the level.
- **Timbre**: the ratios of the $c_n$, set by the sliders $c_1, \dots, c_8$ (bright versus mellow; missing partials); how far the $f_n$ sit from whole-number multiples, set by $B$ (smooth, then shimmer, then clang); and how each partial's size changes over time, especially at the start.[^timbre]
- **Duration**: the fading time, set by the decay, and when the player stops the note.

In the mixer, partial $n$ sits at $n f\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}/\sqrt{1 + B}$, the rule for a stiff string:[^stiff] at $B = 0$ on the whole-number multiples of $f$, and as $B$ grows the higher ones run sharp. With $c_1 = 0$ the lowest partial is at $2f$, yet the pitch stays $f$.

```{=html}

  <canvas id="mxWave" style="height:120px" aria-label="The sound's wave over three cycles of the lowest frequency"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" id="mxSpec" viewBox="0 0 320 90" style="max-width:560px" aria-label="The partials: each frequency as a multiple of the lowest, and its size"></svg>

Every partial fades with the same time τ unless the box is ticked. The mixer holds the power fixed as the sizes move, so they change mostly the timbre; the level alone sets the overall size. The pitch stays <i>f</i> even when <i>c</i><sub>1</sub> = 0. The bell-like preset pushes the partials far off the lines with a large <i>B</i>; a real bell's partials follow a different pattern.</p>

## A clear pitch {#clear-pitch}

A sound has a clear pitch when its partials sit at or very near whole-number multiples of one frequency. A plucked string's partials do, so it gives a note you could hum; a struck drum's don't, so it gives a thud.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="duo">
    <div>
      <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-hook="string">▶ Pluck a string</button></div>
      <svg class="spec" id="rulerString" viewBox="0 0 320 96" aria-label="The frequencies in a plucked string's sound, as multiples of the lowest: they sit on the whole-number lines"></svg>
    </div>
    <div>
      <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-hook="drum">▶ Strike a drum</button></div>
      <svg class="spec" id="rulerDrum" viewBox="0 0 320 96" aria-label="The frequencies in a struck drum's sound, as multiples of the lowest: they fall between the whole-number lines"></svg>
    </div>
  </div>
  <p class="cap">The <em>pitch ruler</em>: gray lines mark 1×, 2×, 3×, … the lowest frequency of each sound, and each blue stem is one partial, taller if it starts stronger. An ideal string at 196 Hz, plucked a fifth of the way along (so 5× is missing), and an ideal round drumhead at 140 Hz, struck a third of the way out. Post 3 computes the string's frequencies and post 4 the drum's; the fading times are modelling choices.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

The reason: partials on the multiples of one frequency add up to a sound that repeats at that rate, and the ear hears the repetition rate as the pitch. Pitch is measured as the frequency of the pure tone that listeners match a sound to.[^pitchdef] Pitch that can carry a melody is heard from about 30 Hz[^pressnitzer] up to about 4 or 5 kHz for pure tones;[^oxenham] call this *the range we hear as pitch*. The partials at 1, 2, 3, … times a frequency are its [harmonics](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#harmonic).

## Why whole numbers repeat {#why-whole-numbers-repeat}

Steady partials add up to a sound that repeats exactly when their frequencies are all whole-number multiples of one frequency. Take two pure tones at 220 and 330 Hz, in the ratio 3 : 2: after two cycles of the lower tone the upper has completed three, so the sum starts again, 110 times a second. At the ratio 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, the sum starts again only after 100 cycles of the lower tone, 2.2 times a second.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button id="r2" class="primary">▶ 2 : 1</button><button id="r15" class="primary">▶ 3 : 2</button><button id="r159" class="primary">▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)</button><button id="rPlay">Play the slider's ratio</button></div>
  <div class="slider"><label for="ratio">Ratio</label><input type="range" id="ratio" min="1" max="3" step="0.01" value="2"><output id="ratioOut">2.00×</output></div>
  <div class="readout" id="ratioMsg"></div>
  <canvas id="ratioWave" style="height:120px" aria-label="Sum of two tones over six cycles of the lower one"></canvas>
  <p class="cap">Two pure tones, the lower at 220 Hz; gray ticks mark its cycles. At 1.59 : 1 the sum lines up only after 100 cycles, far off the right of this picture.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

A signal $p$ is [periodic](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#periodic) with period $P > 0$ if $p(t+P) = p(t)$ for every $t$. The **repetition rate** of a periodic sound is 1 over its shortest period.

::: {.result}
**Precisely.** Let
$$
p(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} c_n\sin(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n),
$$
with distinct frequencies $f_n > 0$ and sizes $c_n \ne 0$. A time $P > 0$ is a period of $p$ exactly when every $f_nP$ is a whole number. So $p$ is periodic exactly when every ratio $f_n/f_1$ is a fraction, and then its shortest period is $1/g$, where $g$ is the largest frequency of which every $f_n$ is a whole-number multiple; its repetition rate is $g$.
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Proof</span>Sinusoids of different frequencies are independent, so a period must fit every partial <span class="needs">integrals of products of sines and cosines, and divisibility</span></summary>

*Lemma.* Let $0 < g_1 < \dots < g_m$, and suppose that $\sum_{j=1}^m \big(\alpha_j\cos(2\pi g_j t) + \beta_j\sin(2\pi g_j t)\big) = 0$ for every $t$. Then every $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_j$ is $0$.

*Proof of the lemma.* For a function $w$, write $\langle w\rangle = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T} w(t)\,dt$ for its long-run average, when the limit exists. For $\gamma \ne 0$, $\int_{-T}^{T}\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\,dt = \sin(2\pi\gamma T)/(\pi\gamma)$ stays bounded as $T$ grows, so $\langle\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\rangle = 0$; and $\langle 1\rangle = 1$. The product formulas $2\cos x\cos y = \cos(x-y) + \cos(x+y)$ and $2\sin x\sin y = \cos(x-y) - \cos(x+y)$ then give, for $a, b > 0$, $\langle\cos(2\pi a t)\cos(2\pi b t)\rangle = \langle\sin(2\pi a t)\sin(2\pi b t)\rangle = \tfrac12$ if $a = b$ and $0$ if $a \ne b$. A product of a sine and a cosine is an odd function, so its integral over $[-T, T]$ is $0$, and so is its average. Multiply the assumed identity by $\cos(2\pi g_j t)$ and average: every term vanishes except $\alpha_j/2$, by the averages just computed, so $\alpha_j = 0$. Multiplying by $\sin(2\pi g_j t)$ gives $\beta_j = 0$ in the same way.

*Proof of the statement.* If every $f_nP$ is a whole number, each sine completes whole cycles in time $P$, so $p(t + P) = p(t)$. Conversely, suppose $p(t+P) = p(t)$ for every $t$. By the identity $\sin(\theta + \delta) - \sin\theta = 2\sin(\delta/2)\cos(\theta + \delta/2)$, with $\theta = 2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n$ and $\delta = 2\pi f_n P$,
$$
0 = p(t+P) - p(t) = \sum_{n=1}^N 2c_n\sin(\pi f_nP)\,\cos\!\big(2\pi f_n t + \varphi_n + \pi f_nP\big).
$$
Expanding each term into $\alpha_n\cos(2\pi f_n t) + \beta_n\sin(2\pi f_n t)$ gives $\alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2 = 4c_n^2\sin^2(\pi f_nP)$. The lemma makes every $\alpha_n$ and $\beta_n$ zero, so $c_n\sin(\pi f_nP) = 0$; since $c_n \ne 0$ by hypothesis, $\sin(\pi f_n P) = 0$, which means $f_nP$ is a whole number. This proves the first sentence.

*The shortest period.* If $p$ has a period $P$, the first sentence makes every $f_nP$ a whole number, so $f_n/f_1 = (f_nP)/(f_1P)$ is a fraction. Conversely, suppose every $f_n/f_1$ is a fraction. Over a common denominator $D$, $f_n = q_n h$ with $h = f_1/D$ and whole numbers $q_n$. Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of $q_1, \dots, q_N$ and $g = dh$; then $f_n = m_ng$ with whole numbers $m_n = q_n/d$ whose greatest common divisor is $1$. By the first sentence, $P$ is a period exactly when every $m_n\,gP$ is a whole number. If $gP$ is a whole number, so is every $m_n\,gP$. Conversely, Bézout's identity (whole numbers whose greatest common divisor is $1$ have a combination with whole-number coefficients equal to $1$) gives whole numbers $u_n$ with $\sum_n u_nm_n = 1$, so $gP = \sum_n u_n\,(m_n\,gP)$ is a whole number. So the periods are exactly the whole-number multiples of $1/g$, and the shortest is $1/g$. Finally, if every $f_n$ is a whole-number multiple of some $g'$, then $1/g'$ is a period, hence a multiple of $1/g$, so $g' \le g$: $g$ is the largest such frequency.

*Check on the examples.* Partials at 440, 660 and 880 Hz have $h = 220$, $q_n = 2, 3, 4$ and $d = 1$, so $g = 220$ Hz although no partial sits there. Tones at 100 and 159 Hz have $g = 1$ Hz: the sum repeats once a second.

</details>
:::

Real partials fade, or sit only near the multiples, so the sound only nearly repeats. Its repetition rate is then the largest frequency $g$ in the range we hear as pitch such that every strong partial lies within a set tolerance of a whole-number multiple of $g$. The tolerance comes from hearing: a low partial mistuned by more than about 1 to 3%, depending on the listener, stands out as a separate tone.[^mgp1] Within 2%, the drum's strong partials in the pitch-ruler demo fit no $g$ above about 20 Hz, below the range we hear as pitch; the string's fit 196 Hz exactly.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The drum's fit at each tolerance, and fading sounds</summary>

Take the partials of the drum in the pitch-ruler demo up to 3.2 times the lowest that start with at least a tenth of the strongest one's size: 1, 1.593, 2.295, 2.653 and 3.155 times 140 Hz. (Its partials at 2.136 and 2.917 start at only about 2% of the strongest's size, because the strike point or the listening point sits near a still line of their modes.) Call a frequency $g$ a fit within a tolerance $\epsilon$ if each partial lies within the fraction $\epsilon$ of a whole-number multiple $kg$ with $k \ge 1$. A computer search over $g$ gives the largest fit; adding the drum's higher partials could only lower it.

| Tolerance | Largest fit $g$ |
|:--|:--|
| 1% | about 14 Hz |
| 2% | about 20 Hz |
| 3% | about 46 Hz |

Within 3%, a base of about 46 Hz fits, as its 3rd, 5th, 7th, 8th and 10th multiples, with nothing at the base or at its 2nd or 4th multiple. That tolerance is generous: the thresholds above are for one mistuned partial among exact harmonics, and here every partial is off at once. In the pitch-ruler demo the sound is a thud.

*Fading sounds.* A sound that dies away cannot repeat exactly: if $p(t+P) = p(t)$ for every $t$, then $p(t) = p(t + rP)$ for every whole number $r$, which tends to $0$ as $r$ grows, so $p$ is zero. It can nearly repeat: if every partial sits on a multiple of $g$ and fades with the same time $\tau$, each period is the one before shrunk by the factor $e^{-1/(g\tau)}$, by 0.45% at $g = 220$ Hz and $\tau = 1$ s.

</details>
:::

## The missing fundamental {#missing-fundamental}

The pitch of a single note (not a chord) is its repetition rate, even when no partial sits there;[^moorepitch] call this the *pitch rule*.


In the mixer, choose *All 1/n*, then *No 1st partial*: the wave changes shape but still repeats every $1/f$ seconds, with $f$ the base frequency, and the pitch stays. Hearing the pitch with no partial at the repetition rate, the [fundamental](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#fundamental), is the *missing-fundamental* effect; it keeps a deep voice's pitch over a telephone line, which carries little below about 300 Hz.[^mf] Keep only $c_2$, $c_4$, $c_6$ and $c_8$, and the pitch jumps an [octave](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#octave).

### Beats {#beats}

Two partials close in frequency are heard as one tone that swells and fades. For two equal pure tones at $f_1$ and $f_2$,
$$
\sin(2\pi f_1 t) + \sin(2\pi f_2 t) = 2\cos\big(\pi (f_2 - f_1) t\big)\,\sin\big(\pi (f_1 + f_2) t\big),
$$
a tone at the average frequency whose size swells and fades $|f_2 - f_1|$ times a second: [beats](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beats).[^moorebeats] Faster beats sound rough, and tones far enough apart sound as two smooth tones.[^pl]

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-beat="2">▶ 220 + 222 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-beat="8">▶ 220 + 228 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-beat="25">▶ 220 + 245 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-beat="110">▶ 220 + 330 Hz</button></div>
  <div class="readout" id="beatRead"></div>
  <canvas id="beatWave" style="height:110px" aria-label="The sum of the two tones over one second"></canvas>
  <p class="cap">The sum of two equal pure tones over one second. At 110 Hz apart the swells come too fast to see here, and you hear two smooth tones.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

### Exceptions to the pitch rule {#exceptions}

The pitch rule fails for three kinds of sound.

*Chords.* C4 and G4 ([note names](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#note-names)) tuned to exactly 3 : 2 together repeat 130.8 times a second, the rate of C3, yet you hear two notes: the ear sorts the partials into two sets of harmonics, with different bases, and hears each set as one sound.[^bregman]

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-s="cC4">▶ C4</button><button class="primary" data-s="cG4">▶ G4</button><button class="primary" data-s="cBoth">▶ C4 and G4 together</button><button data-s="cC3">▶ C3, the pair's repetition rate</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Each note has eight harmonics, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/8: C4 at 261.6 Hz, G4 at exactly 3/2 of that, 392.4 Hz.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

*Bells and kettledrums.* A harmonic subset of the partials sets the pitch, and the ear may choose an octave above that subset's base. A bell is heard roughly an octave below its main partial, the nominal, often with no partial at the pitch heard.[^hibbert] A kettledrum is named an octave above the base its main partials fit.[^timp1]

*Strongly stretched partials.* Partials running sharp of the multiples, as on a stiff piano string, pull the pitch up.[^jaatinen]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The bell's and the kettledrum's partials</summary>

*The bell.* In a well-tuned church bell the main partials, the hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal, sit near 0.5, 1, 1.2, 1.5 and 2 times the prime, and two more, the superquint and the octave nominal, near 3 and 4 times (W. A. Hibbert, [The upper partials of bells](https://www.hibberts.co.uk/the-upper-partials-of-bells/)). The nominal, superquint and octave nominal, nearly in the ratios 2 : 3 : 4, are heard as harmonics of a missing fundamental, the strike note: the pitch the bell is heard at, roughly an octave below the nominal and close to the prime (W. A. Hibbert, [The strike note of bells](https://www.hibberts.co.uk/?p=701), first published in *The Ringing World*, 20 June 2003, p. 586; Wikipedia, [Strike tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_tone)). It can differ from half the nominal by about a quarter of a semitone, and often no partial sits exactly at it (W. A. Hibbert, [What note do we hear when a bell rings?](https://www.hibberts.co.uk/what-note-do-we-hear-when-a-bell-rings/)). Measured from the hum, the main partials sit at 1, 2, 2.4, 3, 4, 6 and 8: whole numbers, except the tierce, a minor third above the prime. Without the tierce they fit the hum as base, yet the bell is heard an octave higher.

*The kettledrum.* A kettledrum's air pulls one set of its modes near 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a base, yet players name the note an octave higher, at the lowest of the set, the drum's principal tone. A kettledrum measured by Benade, tuned to C3, had its principal tone at 130.8 Hz and partials at about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times it, close to 3, 4, 5 and 6 times half of it, together with others off this pattern (HyperPhysics, [The Timpani](https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Music/timpani.html), tabulating A. H. Benade, [*Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics*](https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofmu0000bena), Oxford University Press, 1976). So the set forms a near-harmonic series on C2, 65.4 Hz, yet the drum is named for its principal tone, C3. The drum's many partials off whole-number ratios make its exact pitch hard to pin down (Institute of Musical Acoustics (Wiener Klangstil), University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna, [The Viennese timpani](https://www.mdw.ac.at/iwk/wiener-pauke/?l=en)).

</details>
:::

## Four routes to a clear pitch {#four-routes}

Instruments reach a clear pitch by four routes: modes on the whole numbers by nature, modes moved there by design, off-line partials suppressed, or a drive that repeats.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 320 112" role="img" aria-label="The first three modes of a string: one arc, two halves, three thirds, at 1, 2 and 3 times the lowest frequency"><path class="dash" d="M 40 22 L 280 22"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 7.7 193.6 7.7 280.0 22"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 36.3 193.6 36.3 280.0 22"/><circle cx="40" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="26">1×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 56 L 280 56"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 41.7 116.8 41.7 160.0 56 C 203.2 70.3 236.8 70.3 280.0 56"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 70.3 116.8 70.3 160.0 56 C 203.2 41.7 236.8 41.7 280.0 56"/><circle cx="40" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="60">2×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 90 L 280 90"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 75.7 91.2 75.7 120.0 90 C 148.8 104.3 171.2 104.3 200.0 90 C 228.8 75.7 251.2 75.7 280.0 90"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 104.3 91.2 104.3 120.0 90 C 148.8 75.7 171.2 75.7 200.0 90 C 228.8 104.3 251.2 104.3 280.0 90"/><circle cx="40" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="94">3×</text></svg>
```

1. **By nature: strings and air columns.** A string's $n$-th mode fits $n$ half-waves between its ends (the picture), and waves of every length travel along the string at the same speed, so an ideal [string](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd)'s $n$-th mode swings at exactly $n$ times the lowest frequency. A flute's air column, open at both ends, resonates at every whole-number multiple, and a [clarinet](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#clarinet)'s, closed at the reed, at the odd ones.[^wolfefc]
2. **By design.** A marimba bar's arch, cut underneath, moves its first [overtone](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#partial) from 2.76 times the lowest, for a uniform bar, to 4 times.[^bars]
3. **By suppression.** Some off-line partials die fast: a [kalimba](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#kalimba) tine's overtones, at 6.27 and 17.55 times its lowest, die within a fraction of a second.[^chapman] Others are never started: a strike at a still point of a mode does not set that mode going.
4. **By a repeating drive: bow and breath.** A bow or a breath keeps feeding the motion, which settles into one repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples, whatever the object's own modes.[^wolfehh] A harmonica reed's own overtones are off the lines, yet blown it chops the air into identical puffs ([post 4](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#harmonica)). The object's modes only shape which partials are strong.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">1 · By nature:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rString">▶ Plucked string</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">2 · By design:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rBar276">▶ Uniform bar</button><button class="primary" data-s="rBar4">▶ Undercut bar</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">3 · Suppressed:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rKal">▶ Kalimba tine</button><button data-s="rKalLong">▶ The same, overtones ringing as long</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">4 · Driven:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rReedP">▶ Harmonica reed, plucked</button><button class="primary" data-s="rReedB">▶ The same reed, blown</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Row 2: a bar's lowest two partials at middle C, with the overtone at 2.76 times the lowest (a uniform bar) or at 4 times (an undercut marimba bar); sizes and fading times illustrative. Row 3: a kalimba tine at C5, its overtones fading fast as measured, then the same partials ringing as long as the lowest. Row 4: plucked, the reed has the tine's off-line frequencies; blown, its partials sit at whole-number multiples only.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

## Loudness {#loudness}

Loudness is set mainly by the [sound pressure level](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#spl): 10 [dB](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#decibel) more is ten times the power and sounds about twice as loud.[^stevens1] At the same level, a low tone sounds quieter than a mid-range one.[^iso1]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Decibels, equal-loudness contours and the power law</summary>

The *sound pressure level* is $20\log_{10}(p_{\mathrm{rms}}/20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa})$ decibels (dB), where $p_{\mathrm{rms}}$, the root-mean-square pressure, is the square root of the long-run average of $p(t)^2$. For steady partials, $p_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 = \tfrac12\sum_n c_n^2$, by the averages in the [proof above](#why-whole-numbers-repeat). The *intensity*, the power carried through each square metre, grows as $p_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$, so 10 dB more is ten times the intensity. By the *equal-loudness contours* of ISO 226, which give the level at which pure tones of each frequency sound equally loud to young listeners, a 100 Hz tone needs about 79 dB to match a 1 kHz tone at 60 dB (ISO 226:2023, [*Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours*](https://www.iso.org/standard/83117.html)). At equal intensity, partials spread beyond a certain width in frequency sound louder than partials bunched together (E. Zwicker, G. Flottorp and S. S. Stevens, ["Critical band width in loudness summation"](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1908963), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 29 (1957), 548–557). Loudness grows roughly as the 0.3 power of intensity, so 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud, since $10^{0.3} \approx 2$ (S. S. Stevens, ["On the psychophysical law"](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0046162), *Psychological Review* 64 (1957), 153–181; Wikipedia, [Stevens's power law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevens%27s_power_law)).

</details>
:::

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">Same size of pressure swing:</span><button class="primary" data-s="l100">▶ 100 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-s="l1000">▶ 1000 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-s="l3000">▶ 3000 Hz</button><button data-s="lAll">▶ All three in turn</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Three pure tones with the same size of pressure swing; small laptop and phone speakers make the 100 Hz tone sound even quieter than headphones do.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

[]{#dynamics-and-timbre}**Dynamics change timbre too.** A harder piano blow is brighter as well as louder: the hammer's felt gets harder the more it is squashed, so a fast hammer stays on the string for a shorter time and starts more high partials.[^aj]

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-s="hSoft">▶ Soft blow</button><button class="primary" data-s="hHard">▶ Hard blow</button><button data-s="hSoftUp">▶ Soft blow, turned up</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Middle C on a model piano string. The third button plays the soft blow 10 dB louder, at the hard blow's average level, and it still sounds duller. How fast the partials fall off with number is illustrative, not computed from a model of the felt.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

## Duration {#duration}

A ringing note lasts as long as its fading times allow, unless the player damps it: a key released, a mute, a hand on a drumhead, or a bass drummer's leg or towel.[^aleo]

## Next

As a preview, the $f_n$ and $c_n$ come from the instrument. [Post 2, *From the instrument to your ear*](../from-instrument-to-ear/index.qmd), derives the sound as $p = h \ast F$: copies of $h$, the sound at your ear of one sharp tap on the instrument's body, delayed and scaled by $F(t)$, the input from the vibrating object. [Post 3](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd) writes down the string's [operator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#operator), whose [spectrum](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#spectrum) sets the $f_n$; [post 4](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd) does the same for the other instruments, and the appendix [*When does an equation have a spectrum?*](../when-an-equation-has-a-spectrum/index.qmd) in general.

(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, M = C.models;

  // buffers peak at 0.8 at most, so 0.8 * G * 0.55 = 0.264 stays below the threshold and relative levels are exact.
  var G = 0.6;
  function peakOf(b) { var d = b.getChannelData(0), pk = 0; for (var i = 0; i < d.length; i++) pk = Math.max(pk, Math.abs(d[i])); return pk; }
  function scale(b, s) { var d = b.getChannelData(0); for (var i = 0; i < d.length; i++) d[i] *= s; return b; }
  function toPeak(b, v) { var pk = peakOf(b); return pk > 0 ? scale(b, v / pk) : b; }
  function rmsOf(b, sec) { var d = b.getChannelData(0), n = Math.min(d.length, Math.floor(sec * b.sampleRate)), s = 0; for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) s += d[i] * d[i]; return Math.sqrt(s / n); }
  // synth(segs, dur): segments {t0, t1, parts: [{f, amp, tau}], ramp (s), sharp (2 ms attack), cut: {at, tau}}; tau omitted = steady.
  function synth(segs, dur) {
    var a = C.ac(), SR = a.sampleRate, N = Math.max(1, Math.floor(dur * SR)), b = a.createBuffer(1, N, SR), d = b.getChannelData(0);
    segs.forEach(function (s) {
      var n0 = Math.floor(s.t0 * SR), n1 = Math.min(N, Math.floor(s.t1 * SR)), len = n1 - n0, r = Math.max(1, Math.floor((s.ramp || 0.02) * SR)), ra = s.sharp ? Math.floor(0.002 * SR) : r;
      s.parts.forEach(function (p) {
        if (p.f > SR / 2.3 || !p.amp) return;
        var w = 2 * Math.PI * p.f / SR, dec = p.tau ? Math.exp(-1 / (p.tau * SR)) : 1, e = p.amp;
        for (var n = 0; n < len; n++) { d[n0 + n] += e * Math.sin(w * n); e *= dec; }
      });
      for (var n = 0; n < len; n++) {
        var env = 1;
        if (n < ra) env = 0.5 - 0.5 * Math.cos(Math.PI * n / ra);
        if (len - n < r) env *= 0.5 - 0.5 * Math.cos(Math.PI * (len - n) / r);
        if (s.cut && n / SR > s.cut.at) env *= Math.exp(-(n / SR - s.cut.at) / s.cut.tau);
        d[n0 + n] *= env;
      }
    });
    return b;
  }
  function one(parts, dur, opt) { opt = opt || {}; return synth([{ t0: 0, t1: dur, parts: parts, ramp: opt.ramp, sharp: opt.sharp, cut: opt.cut }], dur); }
  function harm(f, n, amp, odd, tau) { var out = []; for (var k = 1; k <= n; k++) { if (odd && k % 2 === 0) continue; out.push({ f: f * k, amp: amp(k), tau: tau ? tau(k) : 0 }); } return out; }
  function inv(k) { return 1 / k; }
  function play(b, g) { C.play(b, g == null ? G : g); }

  // ---- 1 · the opening pair, on the pitch ruler ----
  var HOOK = {
    string: { parts: function () { return M.violin.partials({ pluck: 0.2 }); }, f: 196, dur: 2.6, svg: "rulerString" },
    drum: { parts: function () { return M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }); }, f: 140, dur: 2.4, svg: "rulerDrum" }

  }
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-hook]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { var h = HOOK[b.getAttribute("data-hook")]; play(C.render(C.toHz(h.parts(), h.f), h.dur)); });
  });

  function timbreSet() {
    if (timbre) return timbre;
    var power = 0.125, d = 1.3; // every steady sound gets sum of amp^2 / 2 = power
    function norm(parts) { var s = 0; parts.forEach(function (p) { s += p.amp * p.amp / 2; }); var k = Math.sqrt(power / s); return parts.map(function (p) { return { f: p.f, amp: p.amp * k, tau: p.tau }; }); }
    var bright = norm(harm(220, 8, inv));
    var set = {
      tPure: one(norm([{ f: 220, amp: 1 }]), d, { ramp: 0.03 }),
      tBright: one(bright, d, { ramp: 0.03 }),
      tHollow: one(norm(harm(220, 8, inv, true)), d, { ramp: 0.03 }),
      tPluck: one(bright.map(function (p) { var n = Math.round(p.f / 220); return { f: p.f, amp: p.amp, tau: 0.9 / (1 + 0.05 * n * n) }; }), 2.2, { sharp: true, ramp: 0.2 })
    };
    var mx = 0; Object.keys(set).forEach(function (k) { mx = Math.max(mx, peakOf(set[k])); });
    if (mx > 0.8) Object.keys(set).forEach(function (k) { scale(set[k], 0.8 / mx); });
    timbre = set; return set;
  }
  function bar(r2) { return [{ f: C4, amp: 1, tau: 1.0 }, { f: C4 * r2, amp: 0.45, tau: 0.45 }]; }
  var hammerCache = null;
  function hammer() {
    if (hammerCache) return hammerCache;
    var soft = C.render(C.toHz(M.piano.partials({ f1: C4, rolloff: 6 }), C4), 2.5), hard = C.render(C.toHz(M.piano.partials({ f1: C4, rolloff: 16 }), C4), 2.5);
    hammerCache = { soft: soft, hard: hard, up: Math.min(0.7, G * rmsOf(hard, 0.5) / rmsOf(soft, 0.5)) };
    return hammerCache;
  }
  var S = {
    l100: function () { play(one([{ f: 100, amp: 0.8 }], 1.2, { ramp: 0.04 })); },
    l1000: function () { play(one([{ f: 1000, amp: 0.8 }], 1.2, { ramp: 0.04 })); },
    l3000: function () { play(one([{ f: 3000, amp: 0.8 }], 1.2, { ramp: 0.04 })); },
    lAll: function () { play(synth([100, 1000, 3000].map(function (f, i) { return { t0: 1.5 * i, t1: 1.5 * i + 1.1, parts: [{ f: f, amp: 0.8 }], ramp: 0.04 }; }), 4.4)); },
    tPure: function () { play(timbreSet().tPure); },
    tBright: function () { play(timbreSet().tBright); },
    tHollow: function () { play(timbreSet().tHollow); },
    tPluck: function () { play(timbreSet().tPluck); },
    cC4: function () { play(toPeak(one(harm(C4, 8, inv), 1.6, { ramp: 0.03 }), 0.8)); },
    cG4: function () { play(toPeak(one(harm(1.5 * C4, 8, inv), 1.6, { ramp: 0.03 }), 0.8)); },
    cBoth: function () { play(toPeak(one(harm(C4, 8, inv).concat(harm(1.5 * C4, 8, inv)), 1.6, { ramp: 0.03 }), 0.8)); },
    cC3: function () { play(toPeak(one(harm(C4 / 2, 8, inv), 1.6, { ramp: 0.03 }), 0.8)); },
    rString: function () { play(C.render(C.toHz(M.violin.partials({ pluck: 0.2 }), 196), 2.6)); },
    rBar276: function () { play(toPeak(one(bar(2.756), 2.4, { sharp: true, ramp: 0.2 }), 0.8)); },
    rBar4: function () { play(toPeak(one(bar(4), 2.4, { sharp: true, ramp: 0.2 }), 0.8)); },
    rKal: function () { play(C.render(C.toHz(M.kalimba.partials({ f1: 523.25 }), 523.25), 2.4)); },

  document.querySelectorAll("[data-s]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { S[b.getAttribute("data-s")](); });
  });

  // ---- 3 · two tones and their ratio ----
  var rs = document.getElementById("ratio"), ro = document.getElementById("ratioOut"), msg = document.getElementById("ratioMsg"), cv = document.getElementById("ratioWave");
  function period(r) { for (var q = 1; q <= 4; q++) { var p = Math.round(r * q); if (Math.abs(p / q - r) < 0.003) return q; } return 0; }
  function wave() {
    var r = parseFloat(rs.value), q = period(r), d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, ctx = cv.getContext("2d"), T = 6;
    ro.textContent = r.toFixed(2) + "×";
    msg.innerHTML = q ? "repeats every <b>" + q + "</b> cycle" + (q > 1 ? "s" : "") + " of the lower tone: <b>" + (220 / q).toFixed(q === 3 ? 1 : 0) + "</b> times a second" : "does not line up within these six cycles";

    for (var k = 0; k <= T; k++) { var x = k / T * W; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x, H - 8 * d); ctx.lineTo(x, H); ctx.stroke(); }
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(0, H / 2); ctx.lineTo(W, H / 2); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); ctx.lineWidth = 2 * d; ctx.beginPath();
    for (var i = 0; i <= W; i++) { var t = i / W * T, y = Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * t) + 0.7 * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * r * t), py = H / 2 - y / 1.75 * (H / 2 - 10 * d); if (i) ctx.lineTo(i, py); else ctx.moveTo(i, py); }

  rs.addEventListener("input", wave);
  function playR() { var r = parseFloat(rs.value); play(toPeak(one([{ f: 220, amp: 1 }, { f: 220 * r, amp: 0.7 }], 2, { ramp: 0.05 }), 0.8)); }
  document.getElementById("r2").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(2); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("r15").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(1.5); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("r159").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(1.59); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("rPlay").addEventListener("click", playR);

  // ---- 2 · the partials mixer ----
  // c_1..c_8 are scaled so that the steady power sum(amp^2)/2 is P0 at level 0 dB; the level alone sets the overall size.
  // Worst case (all eight equal) the peak is sqrt(8 * 2 * P0) = 0.48, and 0.48 * 0.55 stays below core.js's compressor threshold.
  var P0 = 0.0144, NMX = 8, mxc = [1, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8], mxIn = [];
  var mf1 = document.getElementById("mxF1"), mlev = document.getElementById("mxLev"), mB = document.getElementById("mxB"), mdec = document.getElementById("mxDec");
  var mhi = document.getElementById("mxHi"), mbox = document.getElementById("mxC"), mwv = document.getElementById("mxWave"), mspec = document.getElementById("mxSpec"), mread = document.getElementById("mxRead");
  for (var q = 1; q <= NMX; q++) {
    var row = document.createElement("div"); row.className = "slider";
    row.innerHTML = '<label for="mxc' + q + '" style="min-width:1.6rem"><i>c</i><sub>' + q + '</sub></label><input type="range" id="mxc' + q + '" min="0" max="1" step="0.01" style="flex:1 1 5rem"><output id="mxc' + q + 'o"></output>';

  }
  for (var q2 = 0; q2 < NMX; q2++) (function (i) {
    var el = document.getElementById("mxc" + (i + 1)); mxIn.push(el);
    el.addEventListener("input", function () { mxc[i] = parseFloat(el.value); mxRefresh(); });
  })(q2);
  function mxF1v() { return Math.round(110 * Math.pow(4, parseFloat(mf1.value) / 1000)); }   // 110 to 440 Hz
  function mxBv() { var s = parseFloat(mB.value) / 1000; return 0.1 * s * s * s; }             // 0 to 0.1
  function mxTau() { var v = parseFloat(mdec.value); return v >= 100 ? Infinity : 0.1 * Math.pow(40, v / 99); }  // 0.1 to 4 s, then steady
  function mxParts() {
    var f1 = mxF1v(), B = mxBv(), g = Math.pow(10, parseFloat(mlev.value) / 20), s2 = 0, out = [];
    mxc.forEach(function (a) { s2 += a * a; });
    var k = s2 > 0 ? Math.sqrt(2 * P0 / s2) : 0;
    for (var n = 1; n <= NMX; n++) { var r = n * Math.sqrt(1 + B * n * n) / Math.sqrt(1 + B); out.push({ n: n, ratio: r, f: f1 * r, amp: g * k * mxc[n - 1], rel: mxc[n - 1] }); }
    return out;
  }
  var live = null;
  function mxStopNow(rel) {
    if (!live) return;
    var a = C.ac(), now = a.currentTime, m = live.m.gain, v = m.value;
    m.cancelScheduledValues(now); m.setValueAtTime(v, now); m.setTargetAtTime(0, now, rel);
    live.os.forEach(function (o) { try { o.stop(now + 10 * rel + 0.05); } catch (e) {} });
    live = null;
  }
  function mxStart() {
    var a = C.ac(), P = mxParts(), tau = mxTau(), each = mhi.checked && isFinite(tau);
    mxStopNow(0.01);
    var t0 = a.currentTime + 0.02, m = a.createGain(), os = [], gs = [];
    m.gain.setValueAtTime(0, t0); m.gain.linearRampToValueAtTime(1, t0 + 0.008);
    if (isFinite(tau) && !each) m.gain.setTargetAtTime(0, t0 + 0.008, tau);   // one fading time for all

      o.type = "sine"; o.frequency.value = p.f; g.gain.setValueAtTime(p.amp, t0);

    });

    if (isFinite(tau)) setTimeout(function () { if (live === me) mxStopNow(0.02); }, (8 * tau + 0.2) * 1000);
  }
  function mxLive() {
    if (!live) return;
    var now = C.ac().currentTime;
    mxParts().forEach(function (p, i) { live.os[i].frequency.setTargetAtTime(p.f, now, 0.015); if (!live.each) live.gs[i].gain.setTargetAtTime(p.amp, now, 0.015); });
  }
  function gcdN(a, b) { while (b) { var t = b; b = a % b; a = t; } return a; }
  function mxDraw() {
    var P = mxParts(), f1 = mxF1v(), B = mxBv(), tau = mxTau(), lev = parseFloat(mlev.value);
    document.getElementById("mxF1o").textContent = f1 + " Hz";
    document.getElementById("mxLevo").textContent = (lev < 0 ? "−" + (-lev) : "0") + " dB";
    document.getElementById("mxBo").textContent = B === 0 ? "0" : B < 0.01 ? B.toFixed(4) : B.toFixed(3);
    document.getElementById("mxDeco").textContent = isFinite(tau) ? "τ = " + tau.toFixed(tau < 1 ? 2 : 1) + " s" : "steady";
    mxIn.forEach(function (el, i) { el.value = mxc[i]; document.getElementById("mxc" + (i + 1) + "o").textContent = mxc[i].toFixed(2); });
    // the wave over three cycles of f1, drawn so that the same shape at 0 dB would fill the box
    var d = C.fit(mwv), W = mwv.width, H = mwv.height, x = mwv.getContext("2d"), per = 3, ys = [], pk = 0, g = Math.pow(10, lev / 20), S = 2 * W;
    for (var i = 0; i <= S; i++) { var tt = i / S * per / f1, y = 0; P.forEach(function (p) { y += p.amp * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * p.f * tt); }); ys.push(y); pk = Math.max(pk, Math.abs(y)); }
    var sc = pk > 0 ? g * (H / 2 - 8 * d) / pk : 0;
    x.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); x.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); x.lineWidth = d;
    for (var c = 0; c <= per; c++) { var px = c / per * W; x.beginPath(); x.moveTo(px, H - 8 * d); x.lineTo(px, H); x.stroke(); }
    x.beginPath(); x.moveTo(0, H / 2); x.lineTo(W, H / 2); x.stroke();
    x.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); x.lineWidth = 2 * d; x.beginPath();
    ys.forEach(function (y, i) { var px = i / 2, py = H / 2 - y * sc; if (i) x.lineTo(px, py); else x.moveTo(px, py); }); x.stroke();

    C.stems(mspec, P.map(function (p) { return { ratio: p.ratio, amp: p.rel }; }), { W: 320, H: 90, rmax: rmax, fs: 8, sw: 3, labelEvery: rmax > 16 ? 4 : rmax > 10 ? 2 : 1, noOff: true });
    // readout

    } else msg = "partials at " + on.slice(0, 3).map(function (p) { return "<b>" + p.ratio.toFixed(2) + "</b>"; }).join(", ") + (on.length > 3 ? ", …" : "") + " × <i>f</i>: no exact repetition";

  function mxRefresh() { mxDraw(); mxLive(); }
  [mf1, mlev, mB].forEach(function (el) { el.addEventListener("input", mxRefresh); });
  mdec.addEventListener("input", mxDraw);
  mdec.addEventListener("change", function () { if (live) mxStart(); });
  mhi.addEventListener("change", function () { if (live) mxStart(); });
  document.getElementById("mxPlay").addEventListener("click", function () { mxDraw(); mxStart(); });
  document.getElementById("mxStop").addEventListener("click", function () { mxStopNow(0.03); });
  function bSlider(B) { return Math.round(1000 * Math.cbrt(B / 0.1)); }
  var MXP = {
    pure: { c: [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], B: 0, dec: 100, hi: false },
    all: { c: [1, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8], B: 0, dec: 100, hi: false },
    odd: { c: [1, 0, 1 / 3, 0, 1 / 5, 0, 1 / 7, 0], B: 0, dec: 100, hi: false },
    nofirst: { c: [0, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8], B: 0, dec: 100, hi: false },
    piano: { c: [1, 0.55, 0.4, 0.28, 0.2, 0.14, 0.1, 0.07], B: 0.001, dec: 80, hi: true },
    bell: { c: [1, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.45, 0.4, 0.35], B: 0.1, dec: 85, hi: false }
  };
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-mx]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () {
      var p = MXP[b.getAttribute("data-mx")];
      mxc = p.c.map(function (v) { return Math.round(v * 100) / 100; }); mB.value = bSlider(p.B); mdec.value = p.dec; mhi.checked = p.hi;
      mxDraw(); mxStart();
    });
  });

  // ---- 4 · beats ----
  var bc = document.getElementById("beatWave"), bread = document.getElementById("beatRead"), bdf = 2;
  function beatDraw() {
    var d = C.fit(bc), W = bc.width, H = bc.height, x = bc.getContext("2d"), K = 48;
    x.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); x.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); x.lineWidth = d;
    x.beginPath(); x.moveTo(0, H / 2); x.lineTo(W, H / 2); x.stroke();
    x.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); x.lineWidth = Math.max(1, d);

  document.querySelectorAll("[data-beat]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () {

    });
  });

  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { mxDraw(); wave(); beatDraw(); });

})();
</script>
